headline: High-risk shared filesystem and write-capable pair create prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict exposure; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write the user filesystem, and agent_a explicitly shares state with other instances via filesystem. That creates a plausible default bridge for agent_b to ingest agent_a outputs as trusted content, even without clipboard or MCP on B. The interaction is documented in the profiles, so this is not speculative.
conditions: IF agent_a writes instructions or artifacts into a shared cwd that agent_b later reads
IF agent_b treats file contents as authoritative without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate working directories per agent
Add provenance tags to files exchanged between agents
Require manual review before agent_b consumes agent_a outputs
Disable shared filesystem handoff for instruction-bearing files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches source code and files in cwd, while agent_b touches academic papers, metadata, research questions, and configuration secrets. Because both have filesystem access and agent_a shares state via filesystem, sensitive material can flow between them through the workspace even if neither is explicitly exfiltrating. The pairwise leakage path is documented by the profiles.
conditions: IF secrets or sensitive papers are placed in the shared workspace
IF either agent writes outputs containing those data classes back to disk
mitigations: Keep secrets outside the shared workspace
Mount separate read-only inputs for each agent
Redact sensitive files before either agent runs
Use per-agent output directories with access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, install packages, read and write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses. Agent_a also modifies git state, while agent_b runs in a local development environment with docker-compose workflows. Concurrent writes to the same workspace or repo can corrupt state or overwrite each other, and the profiles show no locking mechanism.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory or git repository
IF either agent performs package installation or file writes while the other is active
mitigations: Run agents in separate clones or containers
Serialize write operations with a lock file
Disable git writes for one agent during shared runs
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent execution

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a can produce shell-driven code changes and agent_b is a content-writing/RAG agent with API surfaces for ask, stream, and agentic-ask. If agent_b consumes agent_a output without verification, errors can cascade into downstream text or actions. The profiles do not prove automatic trust, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a-generated files or stdout as source material
IF agent_b forwards those outputs into downstream API calls or generated content without validation
mitigations: Insert a verification step before agent_b consumes agent_a outputs
Require citations or checksums on transferred artifacts
Limit agent_a outputs to machine-readable schemas
Review downstream actions triggered by agent_b

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_b explicitly handles configuration secrets and academic-paper data, while agent_a handles model-provider keys and extension tokens. Both are open-source and docs-only, but the profiles do not state aligned retention, residency, or deletion controls. Because compliance gaps are plausible and not mitigated by default, medium fits; agent_a is cited for its secret handling, and agent_b for its broader data classes.
conditions: IF regulated or personal data is stored in the shared workspace
IF retention or deletion requirements differ between the two environments
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair run
Document retention and deletion rules for both agents
Separate secret stores from working files
Review residency and DPA requirements before deployment
